[00:00] Sofia (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. Quick check, audio ok? 
[00:08] David (Atlas): Yeah we can hear you, thanks. 
[00:12] Marcus (Redwood SE): Hi, I'm Marcus, I'll be doing most of the technical walkthrough today, looped in Sofia for commercial items. 
[00:18] Maya (Atlas): Thanks Marcus. We're mainly interested on how batching + prefix or K-V cache can lower our token cost while keeping 200ms p95 for user-facing chat. 
[00:28] Marcus: Great, that's exactly the usecase we built this Optimize module for. We'll start with a quick overview then go into a cost model and recommended configs. 
[00:36] [00:36] Marcus: So, baseline assumptions — single-turn chat, avg prompt 120 tokens, expected response 80 tokens, peak qps 40, sustained qps about 12 during trading hours. Does that align with what you shared in the questionnaire? 
[00:48] David: Yes that's close. We also have some batch backfill jobs that hit the same models but those are flexible on latency. 
[00:56] Marcus: Excellent. Two levers we usually recommend: intelligent batching at the serving layer, and KV/prefix caching for repeated prefixes — both reduce per-token compute. Batching increases utilization but can add queuing delay, cache reduces compute by short-circuiting forward pass for cached activations. 
[01:16] [01:16] Maya: Quick question — what's the difference between prefix cache and KV cache? People sometimes use the terms interchangeably. 
[01:22] Marcus: Good point. In our terminology prefix cache stores the model's outputs or hidden states for a prompt prefix — basically reusable context. KV cache refers specifically to key/value cache used in transformer attention during decoding. Practically, prefix cache is more coarse-grained; KV cache is runtime-level and can avoid recomputing attention when the prefix repeats across requests. 
[01:40] Liam (SRE): Is this the same as the "K-V cash" I saw in the docs? I think Fireflies mis-transcribed it once. 
[01:45] Marcus: (laughs) Yeah, KV cash is a common misread. It's KV cache. 
[01:48] [01:48] Marcus: Here's a simple cost model example we prepared — assume no caching and minimal batching, your baseline per-million-input-tokens cost with our hosted small model is roughly $120 per 1M tokens (compute + infra). With recommended batching and a 30% cache hit rate, we can push that down to about $40-45 per 1M tokens. With aggressive caching for stable prefixes and dedicated instance pricing, you could see < $25 per 1M tokens in some workloads. 
[02:20] David: That's a big delta. The 30% hit-rate — is that realistic for chat where prompts change a fair bit? 
[02:28] Marcus: It depends on templates. For customer support or financial chat with standardized prompts (e.g., "Get account balance for X"), prefix reuse is high. For open-ended creative prompts it's lower. The Optimize tool takes your sample traces and estimates realistic hit-rates; we've seen 15-40% for mixed workloads. 
[02:46] [02:46] Maya: How does batching affect p95? We need 200ms p95. 
[02:51] Marcus: Batching increases throughput by combining requests into GPU work, but you have to tune the max batch wait time. For p95-sensitive endpoints we recommend: small max batch size (8-16) and tight max wait (5-15ms). That typically keeps p95 within target while reducing compute by ~20-35% depending on utilization. 
[03:14] Sofia: Quick commercial point — if you move to Dedicated, you get better unit economics for steady-state usage and we can give committed throughput guarantees. For pilot we're happy to run hosted with burst/dedicated routing as needed. 
[03:28] [03:28] David: Sound good. For security we need SOC2 plus KMS integration, and VPC peering is a must for us. 
[03:34] Priya (Compliance): Also data residency — European customers need EU region handling, and logs retention policy is important. 
[03:40] Marcus: Understood. We support customer-managed KMS and Private deployments for full VPC/on-prem. We'll include our SOC2 and KMS docs in the follow-up. 
[03:50] [04:00] Marcus: Back to caching: the two main knobs are TTL and signature granularity. TTL governs how long a cached prefix is valid. Signature granularity decides whether you're caching at exact prompt string level or at tokenized normalized templates. We generally normalize user IDs and session tokens to increase hit rates. 
[04:22] Maya: Normalizing sounds risky for us, because prompts include PII sometimes. 
[04:28] Marcus: Absolutely — privacy first. The normalization step should strip or replace PII before normalization; we can do that client-side or within a sanitized proxy. For regulated data, you can restrict caching entirely for PII-containing prompts. 
[04:40] [04:40] David: Can you show the Optimize console quick? 
[04:44] Marcus: Yep, switching to screen share. (brief pause) Ok on the console — top-left you see workload profiles, next the batching suggestions tab. Here's the estimated cost savings chart based on your uploaded trace. You can toggle hit-rate assumptions and see p95 impact. 
[05:05] [05:05] Marcus: For example, toggling batch size to 16 and wait time to 10ms shows theoretical 28% cost reduction with p95 increase from 170ms to 195ms in this simulation. 
[05:18] Maya: That's right on our SLO. What's the margin of error on these sims? 
[05:22] Marcus: We typically cite +/-10-15% depending on how representative the trace is. That's why we recommend running a short pilot benchmark against actual traffic. 
[05:30] [05:30] David: How do you handle cold cache misses for KV cache, particularly for long-tail prompts? 
[05:35] Marcus: We prioritize low-latency by combining cache lookup and model dispatch. On cache miss, request goes to model immediately. For extremely long-tail prompts we fall back to min-batch of 1 to avoid additional queuing. Also there's hybrid strategies: serve short tails from a smaller faster model and route heavy or creative prompts to larger models. 
[05:52] Liam: Is there any extra cost for maintaining cache state? Like memory/redis etc. 
[05:56] Marcus: Good question. For hosted, cache costs are included in the unit economics; for private/dedicated deployments, KV cache memory footprint is on the instance (GPU/host RAM). We provide guidance on sizing — for your median session length we'd estimate ~10-30GB of working KV state for 10-50 concurrent decodes. 
[06:17] [06:17] David: That seems fine. Can you share the spreadsheet numbers you used? 
[06:20] Marcus: I'll share the spreadsheet after the call — it includes assumptions: tokenization, avg prompt/response length, hit-rate, batch wait, and cost per GPU-hour under hosted vs dedicated. 
[06:29] [06:29] Maya: On the topic of model variants and fallback — if a model is unavailable or overloaded, do you automatically fall back to a thinner quantized variant? 
[06:36] Marcus: Yes, smart routing policies can fallback to compatible variants; you can configure acceptable quality thresholds for fallbacks. We also support A/B routing and can have canaries during rollouts. 
[06:48] [06:48] Sofia: Commercial question — what's the expected timeline for a pilot? 
[06:51] Sofia: Typically we can spin a pilot in 1-2 weeks: onboarding, security review, and a 48h benchmark. 
[06:58] David: That's doable. Who on your side owns the pilot run? 
[07:02] Marcus: Marcus and team — we'll run the benchmark with your sample traffic, then produce an Optimize report. 
[07:09] [07:09] Marcus: Quick demo of edge cases — when the prefix includes session-specific tokens we recommend signature rules to strip session ids so the cache can still match template-level prefixes. 
[07:21] Maya: Could that introduce incorrect responses by mixing contexts? 
[07:25] Marcus: If not careful, yes. That's why we recommend only stripping stable identifiers and preserving semantic tokens. We'll help define safe normalization rules during pilot. 
[07:36] [07:36] Priya: For compliance, we'd need audit logs of what was cached and TTLs. Does Redwood provide that? 
[07:42] Marcus: Yes, we surface cache metrics, hit/miss logs (redacted), and you can pipeline audit logs to your SIEM. We'll include retention config in the security pack. 
[07:52] [07:52] David: Any pitfalls you've seen when teams try to DIY? 
[07:56] Marcus: Lots. The common ones: naive batching that increases p99, caching that stores PII, and not accounting for model quality regressions after quantization. Optimize gives guardrails and simulates quality regressions. 
[08:12] [08:12] Marcus: Now, hypothetical numbers for your workload: with modest batching (max batch 12, wait 10ms) and conservative cache hit-rate 20%, estimated monthly savings ~45% on token compute cost; with dedicated and 35% hit-rate maybe 60% savings. 
[08:30] David: If we go with dedicated, what's the commitment look like? 
[08:33] Sofia: For Dedicated we have monthly/annual committed throughput contracts. We can structure a pilot that starts hosted, then a 3-month reserved for Dedicated if the pilot hits the expected metrics. We'll send contract templates. 
[08:45] [08:45] Marcus: One more technical note: prefix cache TTL should be tied to domain drift. For financial Q&A the prefix templates are stable week-to-week, so longer TTLs (hours to days) can be safe, but for dynamic market data you probably don't want caching across minutes unless you have fine-grained invalidation. 
[09:06] Maya: How do you measure cache efficacy during pilot? 
[09:10] Marcus: We report hit-rate, average tokens saved per request, latency delta, and quality regressions on a held-out eval set derived from your prompts. 
[09:19] [09:19] Marcus: Quick interjection — any concerns about model hallucination increasing with caching? 
[09:23] David: Yeah, worried about stale context causing wrong answers. 
[09:26] Marcus: Caching doesn't invent answers, but stale cached outputs could return outdated info. That's why TTLs and invalidation hooks are crucial; we recommend cache warmers and invalidation tied to events (e.g., account update). 
[09:40] [09:40] Sofia: Ok let's talk timeline and owners — I'll send pricing and pilot agreement, Marcus will run the benchmark, Atlas provides traces and compliance requirements. 
[09:50] David: One last question on encryption: we need customer-managed keys and field-level encryption for logs, is that supported? 
[09:56] Marcus: Yes, we support CMK (customer-managed keys) and can offer field-level redaction in logs before export. We'll include technical notes in the security pack. 
[10:08] [10:08] Marcus: Any other questions on the Optimize recommendations? 
[10:12] Maya: Not right now. We might want a deeper session on quantization tradeoffs since we have some latency-sensitive microservices. 
[10:19] Marcus: Happy to run that; suggest a dedicated SE session for quantization & kernel-level perf. 
[10:25] [10:25] David: Can you also show what happens if we increase batch size to 32? We want to understand tail risk. 
[10:30] Marcus: Sure — toggling to 32 increases throughput but p95 jumps in the sim to ~280ms and p99 to >400ms for some spikes. Not viable for user-facing endpoints; good for backfill though. 
[10:44] [10:44] Marcus: I'll note that as a follow-up to include in the spreadsheet: sensitivity analysis for batch sizes.
